ownership.label: Ownership & moves
ownership.blurb: Every value has exactly one owner. Passing or assigning by value moves it, and the old name can no longer be used. The value is dropped when its owner goes out of scope.

borrowing.label: Borrowing & slices
borrowing.blurb: &T is a shared, read-only loan; &mut T is an exclusive one. Slices (&[u8], &str) are borrowed views into a buffer somebody else owns.

items.title: Ch. 1 Foundations — “Borrowing and Lifetimes”: Shared References, Mutable References
Ch. 2 Basic Types — “Arrays, Vectors, and Slices”

lifetimes.label: Lifetimes
lifetimes.blurb: A lifetime is the compiler's name for how long a borrow stays valid. Annotations like <'a> change no behaviour; they say which input an output borrows from.

items.title: Lifetimes → Static
items.note: what 'static really means in a bound

smart-pointers.label: Box, Rc, Arc & Drop
smart-pointers.blurb: Box<T> is one owner of a heap value. Rc<T> and Arc<T> share ownership through a reference count; Arc is the thread-safe one. Drop runs cleanup at a known point.

items.title: Ch. 15 Smart Pointers (15.1 Box, 15.3 Drop, 15.4 Rc)
Std library types → Box, stack and heap
Ch. 2 Types — “Dynamically Sized Types and Wide Pointers”
items.note: why Arc<dyn Trait> is two words wide

interior-mutability.label: Interior mutability
interior-mutability.blurb: How code holding only a shared reference (&self) can still change things: Mutex and RwLock guard the data itself, atomics update single numbers, OnceLock initialises exactly once.

items.title: 15.5 RefCell<T> and the Interior Mutability Pattern

concurrency.label: Threads, Send & Sync
concurrency.blurb: Send means a value may move to another thread; Sync means it may be shared between threads. The compiler checks both, which is why shared state is wrapped in Arc<Mutex<…>>.

items.title: 16.4 Extensible Concurrency with Send and Sync
Ch. 10 Concurrency (and Parallelism) — “Concurrency Models”: Shared Memory, Worker Pools, Actors

items.note: Send and Sync are marker traits

async.label: async/await & tokio
async.blurb: An async fn returns a Future that does nothing until it is polled. tokio polls thousands of them on a few threads. A spawned task must own everything it uses ('static).

items.title: Ch. 8 Asynchronous Programming — “Ergonomic Futures”, “Pin and Unpin”, “Tying It All Together with spawn”

methods.label: Methods & self
methods.blurb: impl blocks, receivers (&self, &mut self, self) and what the dot desugars to.

items.title: 10.2 Traits — implementing a trait on a type
Ch. 3 Designing Interfaces — “Borrowed vs. Owned” (choosing self, &self, &mut self)

traits-generics.label: Traits, generics & dyn
traits-generics.blurb: Traits are interfaces. Generics (T: Trait) are resolved at compile time; dyn Trait is resolved at run time through a vtable, like a Java interface call.

items.title: 18.2 Using Trait Objects to Abstract over Shared Behavior
Ch. 2 Types — “Traits and Trait Bounds” (Compilation and Dispatch)
Ch. 3 Designing Interfaces — “Object Safety”, “Borrowed vs. Owned”

enums-patterns.label: Enums & pattern matching
enums-patterns.blurb: Rust enums carry data per variant, like Kotlin sealed classes, and match must cover every case. Most state machines in this codebase are enums.

items.title: Ch. 6 Enums and Pattern Matching (incl. 6.3 if let and let…else)
Ch. 2 First Steps with Rust — “Categorizing with Enumerations”
Ch. 3 Build Your First Game with Rust — “Creating Different Game Modes”

error-handling.label: Result, ? and panics
error-handling.blurb: Errors are values: Result<T, E>. The ? operator returns early and converts the error with From. A panic is a crash, and with panic = "abort" it takes the host process with it.

items.title: Ch. 9 Error Handling (9.2 Result, 9.3 To panic! or Not to panic!)
Ch. 4 Error Handling — Enumeration vs. Opaque Errors, Propagating Errors
Ch. 2 Test for Echo — “Using the Result Type”; Ch. 4 Head Aches — “Converting Strings into Errors”

iterators-closures.label: Iterators & closures
iterators-closures.blurb: Iterator chains are lazy, like Kotlin sequences. Closures borrow what they capture unless they are marked move, in which case they take ownership.

items.title: Ch. 13 Functional Language Features: Iterators and Closures
Ch. 5 Word to Your Mother — “Iterating the Files”

modules-cargo.label: Crates, modules & features
modules-cargo.blurb: A workspace holds crates, and each crate is a tree of modules. Cargo features and #[cfg] switch code on or off at compile time.

items.title: Ch. 5 Project Structure — Features, Workspaces, Conditional Compilation
Ch. 5 Build a Dungeon Crawler — “Dividing Your Code Into Modules”
Ch. 1 Truth or Consequences — “Organizing a Rust Project Directory”

unsafe-ffi.label: unsafe & FFI
unsafe-ffi.blurb: unsafe marks code whose memory safety you vouch for yourself. At an FFI boundary the compiler cannot see who owns what, so every allocation needs an agreed owner and a matching free.

items.title: 20.1 Unsafe Rust (incl. “Using extern Functions to Call External Code”)
Ch. 11 Foreign Function Interfaces — “Types Across Language Boundaries”, “Allocations”, “Safety”

macros.label: Macros & attributes
macros.blurb: println!, vec!, #[derive(…)], #[tokio::main] and #[uniffi::export] are code generators that run at compile time.

testing.label: Tests
testing.blurb: #[test] functions live next to the code (unit tests) or in tests/ (integration tests that see only the public API). #[ignore] keeps live-network tests out of the default run.

items.title: Ch. 11 Writing Automated Tests (11.2 Running, 11.3 Organization)

bytes-strings.label: Bytes, strings & formatting
bytes-strings.blurb: String owns UTF-8 text and &str borrows it. Vec<u8>, [u8; N] and &[u8] are the byte versions. Most protocol code in this project is byte slicing.

items.title: 8.2 Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings
Ch. 2 Basic Types — “String Types”: Byte Strings, Strings in Memory
Ch. 4 Head Aches — “Reading Bytes Versus Characters”

cli.label: Binaries, CLIs & signals
cli.blurb: A binary crate has a main(); daemons parse arguments, report errors with anyhow and shut down cleanly on Ctrl-C.

items.title: Ch. 2 Test for Echo — “Parsing Command-Line Arguments Using clap”
